answers.text: It’s fine to have a non-Jew pray in a synagogue. This was even done in the Temple itself. When King Solomon dedicated the Temple, he specifically asked that God hear the prayers of non-Jews who come to the Temple to pray (I Kings 8:41-43). Thus, as long as the visitor believes in a monotheistic religion such as Christianity or Islam – so that he’s praying to the same God as we, there is no reason to object to his prayers. (See also Shulchan Aruch O.C. 156:1.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Grandson Sitting Shiva, Saying Kaddish
questions.question: I had a painful, turbulent childhood and have had a much closer relationship with my grandparents, who provided some much-needed security in my life and help raise me up. Unfortunately, my grandfather will not be around much longer. Can I or should I sit shiva for my grandfather – in addition to or instead of my father? Also, should I take on saying Kaddish for him?

answers.text:
I’m sorry to hear of your situation. Customarily, we do not sit shiva for a grandparent, only for an immediate relative. In your case in particular, doing so would be an affront to your true parents. Even if they are wicked and there is no mitzvah to honor them, you should still avoid hurting their feelings. You should instead find other ways to honor your grandfather’s memory after his passing, such as studying extra Torah, especially Mishna, for the elevation of his soul.
In terms of Kaddish, a grandson is generally a good choice to say Kaddish if the son is not able to. But since your parents are still alive, you would have to first receive their permission to say Kaddish in their lifetime.
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Concept of Tumah (Uncleanness), Niddah
questions.question: What is the idea that women become tamei when they menstruate? Does the Torah view a woman as lowly or filthy just because of a natural process beyond her ability to control?

answers.text:
No, not at all. The notion of tumah – spiritual uncleanness – has nothing to do with physical hygiene and certainly not Jewish misogyny. It is a much more general concept – one which also applies to women but which is not at all limited to them.
There are many situations which create tumah. Some of the primary ones are:
A dead body. Certain dead animals. A leper (metzora). A man who has an emission. A man who has a gonorrheal flow (zav). A woman after childbirth. A woman who has a period (niddah) – especially if much earlier than its expected time (zavah). Certain types of contact with the ashes of the Red Cow.
The laws of tumah are extremely complex – so much so that I would not even attempt the briefest summary of them here – how tumah is transmitted, how it applies to food and utensils, its many gradations and indirect forms, the restrictions applying to a tamei person or item, how tumah applies to terumah (tithes given to the Priests) and kodshim (sacred items), the purification process, the vast world of extensions the Rabbis of the Talmud made to these principles, etc. Suffice it to say that most students of the Talmud shudder when they approach a section of the Talmud discussing such topics.
There is, however, one underlying concept which I would like to share – in response to your question. Fundamentally, tumah represents a spiritual void. When holiness departs this world, the resultant loss of sanctity creates a type of vacuum – an emptiness from the sanctity which had previously been present. And just as nature abhors a vacuum, so too such a spiritual void cannot exist. It thus becomes filled with its opposite – tumah / impurity.
This is most evident in the case of a dead body. A living person has the ability to serve God and sanctify himself. After he dies, his soul ascends to Heaven and only his lifeless corpse remains. That body, which has now lost its ability to attain holiness, becomes tamei. This is likewise true of a dead animal (unless it was slaughtered and made kosher). A dead animal has a much lower level of tumah – since its previous potential for and subsequent loss of holiness was much lesser to begin with.
The same is true of a woman after childbirth. Before her baby was born, an expectant mother contained within her a new life – a separate being which had its own potential for sanctity and spiritual growth. Now – although a healthy baby was hopefully born – the mother herself lacks the same degree of life she had earlier possessed, and that lack gives rise to tumah. Interestingly, the Torah teaches us that a postpartum mother contracts tumah for a lengthier period of time if she gives birth to a girl than if she has a boy (Leviticus 12). The reason for this is clear: When she was pregnant with a girl, she contained not only a life inside of her, but a girl who herself could potentially create more life. Thus, the tumah engendered when her baby left her is in a sense twice the tumah she contracts when she has a boy – who lacks the same ability to create new life.
Lastly, a woman who has a period suffers a similar type of loss. Beforehand, her body had prepared a lining which had the potential to carry a pregnancy and new life. Since, however, she did not conceive, the potential for life in her body is flushed away and discharged. This too represents a loss of potential life – and is cause for tumah. (It’s interesting to note that the entire phenomenon of menstruation is practically unique to human beings (and several primates). When most other animals become fertile but do not conceive, the additional blood lining their uterus is simply – and much more efficiently – reabsorbed into the body. Only human beings suffer Eve’s punishment that conception and childbirth are much more difficult today (Genesis 3:16). To a lesser extent, the same is true of a man who has an emission (even in the context of marital relations) – who too has lost some of the potential to create life his body had earlier contained.
Secular scholars generally assume that Judaism’s notion of niddah is a throwback to the taboo many primitive cultures placed on women during menstruation – who feared such women were under the influence of dark spirits or the like. But a proper understanding of the detailed laws of tumah demonstrates the profound wisdom of such Torah concepts.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Juror – Capital Crime
questions.question: I am likely to be selected as a juror on a capital case. I was given a questionnaire to fill out, and one of the questions was if I have any beliefs which would conflict with my ability to vote for or against the death penalty. I answered that I do not. But after the fact, I’m wondering if this would be in issue. Secular courts obviously do not follow Torah law. Does that preclude me from serving on one, especially in a capital case?

answers.text:
It is fine and appropriate for you to serve on such a jury. Secular governments are obligated to set up a justice system, and they have the prerogative to enact laws as they see fit in order to preserve law and order. We are further obligated to participate in and cooperate with the local law enforcement, to minimize crime among the general population. This is even so if it means that capital punishment might be the verdict.
(Sources: Rambam Melachim 9:1; Mishnah Halachot, IX 396; see more generally Igrot Moshe, C.M. II 68 for a halachic perspective on capital punishment.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Hat and Jacket for Prayers
questions.question: What do many Orthodox Jews wear black hats? Is there a basis for it in Jewish law?

answers.text:
The common practice of many segments of the Orthodox community to wear a black hat today, especially for prayers, is a combination of Jewish law (halacha) and societal norms.
In terms of halacha, we are obligated to dress respectably when we pray. The verse states: “Prepare to meet your God, Israel” (Amos 4:12). The Talmud (Shabbos 10a), taking this phrase out of its simple context, derives that we must properly prepare ourselves before we pray, recognizing that we are about to stand before the King of kings. We must therefore dress as we would if we would be standing before an important person. This does not mean we must dress in our absolute best finery, but that we dress in a dignified manner – certainly not in shorts, swimwear, a robe, pajamas, etc. We must also wear socks and shoes (in societies where such is considered respectable dress – Shulchan Aruch O.C. 91:5). Several authorities describe the appropriate dress as how a respectable person would be attired while walking in public.
(Note that all of the above is referring to our daily prayers – and in particular its central components – Shema and Shemoneh Esrei. For brief prayers and blessings we say throughout the day, such as blessings on food, it is sufficient to be much more minimally covered.)
In terms of a jacket, the Gemara we cited above illustrates the principle of “Prepare to meet your God” with a sage who would fully dress and “wrap himself” before praying (see similarly Shulchan Aruch 91:6). The apparent meaning is that he wore an extra layer during prayers. Recent authorities recommend that this best be fulfilled with a dress jacket (Laws of Daily Living, Vol. 1, p. 69).
What about a hat? R’ Avraham Danzig (1748-1820), the head of the rabbinical court in Vilna, in elaborating these laws, writes that one must pray wearing a hat – in the manner he would walk in the street (Chayei Adam 22:8). Mishna Berurah (91:12) follows this ruling, adding that we would never stand before an important person not attired in a hat. More contemporary authorities have noted that such arguments hail from a time in which a hat was considered proper attire – a mode of dress which went out of fashion in the 1960’s (see e.g., Laws of Daily Living, Vol. 1, p. 70). Nevertheless, in many religious circles such “fashions” have remained in practice until today – in part to maintain past traditions, and in part so as not to allow non-Jewish standards to determine proper Jewish dress. (There are also Kabbalistic reasons to have two coverings on one’s head, in particular during prayers.) Thus, in many Orthodox circles, hats and jackets are still very much in practice. Not only are they worn for prayers, but as a general mode of dress they are still very much de rigeur.
There is a final interesting halachic consideration regarding wearing a hat. The Shulchan Aruch (O.C. 98:4) writes that prayer is akin to bringing an offering in the Temple, and that just as the Temple Priests wore special clothes, so too a person should preferably have a set of especially nice garments to change into for prayer. (He admits that such would be beyond the means of many.) Thus, wearing a hat for prayers would be a way of fulfilling the custom of wearing a special garment for prayers.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Selling a Sefer Torah (Torah Scroll)
questions.question: Our synagogue has several older Torah scrolls which are in need of repair and we never use. Someone recently approached us about buying one of them (as is). Are we allowed to sell it – using the money for synagogue upkeep?

answers.text:
A Sefer Torah is considered the most sacred item in Judaism today. In general, the Talmud teaches us, we may only sell a sacred item to buy something even more sacred. (For example, one may sell a scroll of one of the Prophets for a Torah scroll, or a synagogue to buy an ark (where the Torah scrolls are placed).) A single exception is that a person who has a privately-owned Torah may sell it to enable him to study Torah or marry.
Since there is nothing more sacred than a Torah scroll, technically speaking, there is nothing it can be sold for. But in practice, a lesser-quality Sefer Torah may be sold for a nicer one. Since, however, you wrote that the Torah scrolls under discussion are in need of repair and presumably not valid, they have a lesser sanctity. Therefore, they can be sold if the money will be used to repair other scrolls in the synagogue’s possession. The money should be carefully set aside (or kept track of), and used for such a purpose alone and not regular synagogue expenses.
(Sources: Mishna Megillah 3:1; Shulchan Aruch O.C. 153:2-4,10; Mishna Berurah there; Igros Moshe Y.D. III 113.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Disposing Old Tzitzit
questions.question: How do I discard an old pair of tzitzit – or strings which fall off of them?

answers.text:
Tzitzit are not considered sacred in the same manner as actual sacred items such as a Torah or religious book. However, the tzitzit strings, since they were used for a mitzvah, should not be treated with disdain. Therefore, tzitzit strings should not be thrown directly into the garbage. A common practice is to first place them in a closed opaque bag (or to double-bag them) and then throw them out. It is also acceptable to leave them near a garbage bin, even though you know that workers will later throw them out. (It’s common to see this after Sukkot every year with s’chach, the foliage used to cover the Sukkah, which people leave outside near the garbage but not in it.)
For tzitzit, many have a nicer practice of placing them in genizah (shaimos) – to be buried together with worn religious books and the like. Some will also save a shorn string to be used as a bookmark (in a Torah book) – based on the reasoning that since it was once used for a mitzvah, it should continue to be used for a mitzvah.
Note that the garment which contains the tzitzit strings has even less sanctity since it is really just an article of clothing like a shirt or a blouse. Only the strings must be treated respectfully when you discard them. Even so, when a garment wears out, you should not use it in an especially disrespectful way – such as to wipe up dirt or use it as a rag. However, after you take off the strings, you may certainly throw it into the garbage as regular.
One further concern with discarding an old pair of tzitzit is that it’s considered improper to ruin kosher tzitzit strings even if you no longer plan to use them. Therefore, you should not simply cut them off the corners of the garment. Ideally, you should carefully untie the old strings to take the off the worn garment. However, rather than such a time-consuming endeavor, it is also acceptable to cut the corners of the garment itself – cutting until you reach the hole that the strings hang from. You can then simply pull off the strings, discard them carefully, and throw out the garment.
One further point is that a tallit – the larger four-corner garment we wear specifically in the synagogue and for prayers, does have a level of sanctity since it is designated for use together with prayer. Therefore, not only its strings, but the garment itself should be disposed of more respectfully. There is no custom to put it in genizah as with tzitzit strings; however, it should not be thrown directly into the garbage, but first placed inside its own bag.
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch O.C. 21:1-2 with Rema, Mishna Berurah 21:7,8,12,13;15:3.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Shiva – After Shabbat
questions.question: Unfortunately, I’m sitting shiva for my mother right now. I know shiva is not observed on Shabbos. What happens after Shabbos?

answers.text:
First of all, I’m very sorry for your loss. In terms of Jewish law, it is as you wrote – that as soon as Shabbat ends, assuming the seven days of shiva continue until at least Sunday, you immediately return to mourning. Thus, unlike on Shabbat where you go to synagogue for prayers, the Saturday night prayers (ma’ariv) will be at your home. As soon as nightfall arrives, you should conclude Shabbat by saying “Baruch ha’mavdil bein kodesh l’chol” (“Blessed is He who distinguishes between the holy and the mundane”). You then switch back to your torn clothes from the week. (Remember to change out of your Shabbat shoes as well.) Shortly after, people will come to your home to hold services. As during the rest of the week, you should lead the services if you know how. (If the minyan is gathered the first moment after Shabbat, then the mourner just takes off his shoes now and only changes his clothes after, with many waiting till right after Havdalah.)
Prayers on Saturday night are as regular for a shiva house except that Psalm 16 is recited at the end (instead of 49 as during the week). Also, the extra prayer of "Vayiten licha…" which many say and which contains many beautiful verses about the blessings we hope to receive during the week, is not said. Also, if possible, Kiddush Levanah (the blessing recited on the new moon) is delayed until after shiva (if after the week will not be too late).
After the services is Havdalah, said at the conclusion of Shabbat. It’s best if someone else can say it for you. If no one else is available, you can say it, but you should skip the introductory verses (since a mourner may not study Torah) and start with the blessings themselves.
May your proper shiva observance be a merit for your mother’s soul.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Soup with Noodles or Croutons
questions.question: What bracha (blessing) do you say on soup with croutons?

answers.text:
It depends on a few factors. Normally, when two foods are mixed and eaten together, a blessing is recited on the primary food alone – which here is clearly the soup. The exception to this is foods made out of the five grains (wheat, barley, oats, rye, spelt). These grains, which in Jewish law are considered the staples of a typical diet, are almost by definition considered primary. When they are made into bread, they are the primary food of the meal, and once we recite ha’motzi on them, we do not make blessings on most of the other foods of our meal. Even when the five grains are made into foods other than bread – such as pasta or croutons, they retain a degree of primacy. They are usually considered the primary food of a mixture, and we recite a bracha on them alone.
Soup is a little more complicated because the noodles and croutons are typically added only to enhance the flavor and/or texture of the soup and are clearly not the main part of the dish. It therefore depends how many you add to your bowl. Here are the basic rules.
(1) If you add a significant amount of soup nuts to your soup and are interested in eating those as well, then you say mezonot alone. The soup nuts, since they are from the five grains, become primary and exempt the rest of the soup. Note that this is true even if you get a spoonful here or there without any croutons. We view the entire food as a single mixture – even the parts of it which do not contain the main ingredient. Even so, when you take your first spoonful and recite the blessing, you should make sure that spoon contains at least some croutons.
(2) If your main intention is the soup, and you just add a relatively small amount of croutons to enhance it and improve the texture, then you say two blessings – she’hakol on the soup and mezonot on the croutons. Although ordinarily we recite a single bracha on a mixture – on the primary ingredient alone, since five-grain foods are always significant, the soup nuts (or noodles) are not included in the other bracha but require their own. An additional point is that in this case you should first say the she’hakol on the rest of the soup (taking a spoonful without croutons) and only after mezonot on the croutons. The reason is because there is a possibility that the mezonot covers the soup, so if you’d say mezonot first, you would no longer be able to say she’hakol on the soup. (It’s even better to say a she’hakol on a different food altogether since again, there is a possibility that the soup really doesn’t require its own bracha.)
(3) If the croutons or noodles are very insignificant, you should not say a bracha on them at all. This could be the case if you are served a bowl of soup with a couple of noodles in it that you hardly notice and certainly don’t consider a significant part of it. Another example is if you’re given soup with a tiny sprinkling of croutons at the top – seemingly more there for decorative purposes than to actually add to the dish.
Before closing, let’s quickly address two other relevant issues. What is the bracha on the soup itself? Chicken soup and meat soup will generally be she’hakol (although again if they come with noodles, the above rules would apply to them). Vegetable soup will generally be ha’adama, but if it’s a watery broth or the vegetables are pureed, she’hakol.
Lastly, chicken soup in particular is generally eaten as part of the Friday night Shabbat meal. Since that meal begins with challah and ha’motzi, we do not recite a bracha on the main course foods eaten in that meal at all, including the soup.
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch O.C.205:2, 208:2; Mishna Berurah 205:11, 208:23; V’Zos HaBracha, pp. 117-118.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Sleeping Alone at Night
questions.question: Is there any problem with sleeping in an empty house?

answers.text:
Potentially. The Talmud (Shabbat 151a) writes that one should not sleep alone for Kabbalistic reasons. This applies if you live alone. Even if there are other people in the house but you have your own room, you should keep your door unlocked (unless that causes a yichud (seclusion) issue with a woman in the house). However, if light enters your room, the issue does not apply.
(Sources: Eishel Avraham O.C. 239; Mishna Berurah 239:8, Sha’ar HaTziyun 17; B’Tzel HaChochma IV 76.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Prayer Versus Accepting God’s Will
questions.question: If everything God does is for the best, why do we pray to God – asking Him to change our fate? Shouldn’t we accept that whatever God grants us is right for us and not ask that things be different? Isn’t prayer basically a rejection God’s will?

answers.text:
Thank you for your profound question. Even though we do accept that God gives us what is right for us, there are three primary reasons why we still pray:
(1) Many of the blessings we deserve in life God does not grant to us automatically and immediately. We must first pray for them to receive them. Our prayers open up the gates of Heavens and bring down the blessings we deserve.
(2) Even if we do not deserve a certain blessing, the very fact that we are turning to God in prayer and asking Him for it might make us worthier and more deserving of it. Thus, our prayers may grant us more than we would otherwise deserve.
(3) A variation of this is that sometimes even with prayer we do not actually deserve a certain blessing. Even so, God may respond favorably to our prayers simply because we turned to Him and asked for it. This is something you might be familiar with if you have small children – or remember from being one yourself. Sometimes, parents would normally turn down a request from their child – yet they might say yes anyway “because you asked so nicely” – teaching their child just how admirable it is when he speaks nicely and places his trust in his parents. God too is our loving Parent who responds to our wishes and may go so far as to change our decree for the better because of our sincere prayers.
Thus, even though we always accept that God gives us what is right for us, we pray for our needs as well – sometimes because the blessings we deserve only come through prayer, and sometimes because our very prayers make us more worthy of further blessings. All the same, we do accept that God knows what is best for us. Thus, if our prayers are not answered in the way we would like, our reaction must be to accept that God knows best, and what we’re asking for is clearly not truly right for us. But of course – viewing the other side of the coin – perhaps our prayers were turned down only because we didn’t pray hard enough for what we wanted – or improve ourselves in other ways to be deserving of such blessing. Thus, although we accept that God knows best, we can and should continue to pray for that which we feel we need.
Of course, at a point, we should probably adopt more of an acceptance mindset rather than a prayer mindset. If after years of heartfelt prayer God still does not grant us the blessings we desire, we should probably focus more on accepting God’s will – that He knows that what we want is simply not right for us – rather than refusing to accept that and continuing to forcefully pray. In any event, if our prayers are turned down, our attitude must never be that God is ignoring us and is insensitive to our needs. We must always approach prayer with the frame of mind that God might be saying no only because He knows what we want is not truly best for us – and that may well be for reasons only He understands.
This also touches on another fundamental question. If God knows our needs – even better than we do ourselves – why does He want us to pray to Him at all? Why ask God for what we think we need – which in fact might be wrong? Why not just leave it entirely up to Him?
The answer in a word is because God wants our prayers. He wants us to talk to Him and ask Him for our needs – not just leave it up to Him and never communicate with Him. He also wants us to go through the internal process of deciding what we feel we need and understanding ourselves better. I discuss this in a different response. Please see here for a further discussion.
Here are also a few nice articles on the general concept of prayer:
May God answer all your prayers for the good!
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Using Ma’aser (Tithe) Money for Torah Study Program
questions.question: I am a retiree and did not study Torah when I was young. Could I use my ma’aser money (the tithe of our income we give to charity) to join a learning program which I would benefit from?

answers.text:
Much success in your studies first of all! In general, ma’aser must be given to others, not spent on ourselves, even for a worthy cause. However, there is room for leniency in a situation where you would otherwise not attend the program at all because of the cost. The same is true of any non-obligatory mitzvah you would not otherwise be able to perform. The reasoning is because we may not use ma’aser for our obligations, but a program you would not have joined is viewed as an extra mitzvah rather than a basic obligation. However, even if you rely on this leniency, you may only give up to 50% of your ma’aser for your own mitzvos. The rest should be given directly to the poor.
If the money you are using to pay for this program is additionally helping support the poor (i.e., the teacher of your program is needy and depends on the income it generates), then you can certainly pay for it from ma’aser (if you can’t afford to attend otherwise).
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch Y.D. 249:1; Tzitz Eliezer IX 1:1-5; The Laws of Tzedakah and Maaser (ArtScroll), pp. 153-155.)
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Earliest Time for Mincha, Said Too Early
questions.question: What is the earliest time you can pray Mincha? And what if you said it too early?

answers.text:
The Mincha prayer corresponds to the daily afternoon Tamid offering brought in the Temple. The earliest time that could be brought was at the start of the afternoon, when the sun first moves to the west of the meridian and its shadows begin to tilt towards the east. This is considered to occur only half an hour after midday (measuring from sunrise to sunset), when such shadows are noticeable. (We are further stringent in the summer to count this half hour relative to the length of the day, considering one hour to be 1/12’th of daylight.) Thus, the earliest time for Mincha is approximately half an hour after astronomical midday, and a bit longer than 30 minutes later in the summer.
However, some authorities maintain that the afternoon Tamid can be offered immediately after midday, not only 30 minutes later. Thus, if you recited Mincha right after midday, it would also count and you wouldn’t repeat Mincha. However, if you prayed before midday entirely, it would not count at all and must be repeated.
You can find accurate halachic times for virtually all locations worldwide at MyZmanim (aish.com retrieves Shabbat times from there as well).
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch 233:1, Mishna Berurah 2 with Sha'ar Tziyun 6, 8.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Non-Jewish Cook for Elder Care
questions.question: We’re arranging for my mother to receive homecare. Is there a problem if her non-Jewish help does the cooking for her as well? We would ensure that the help is aware of the laws of kashrut.

answers.text:
There would definitely be an issue with that. Apart from the laws of kashrut themselves, there is a very early rabbinical decree known as bishul akum – forbidding eating food cooked by a non-Jew. The Sages forbade this in order to safeguard against Jews and non-Jews becoming too friendly and intermarrying. There are some exceptions to this rule: It only applies to relatively important foods, which would be served at a regal meal, and to foods which are inedible raw. Nevertheless, clearly, a Jew may not have a non-Jewish cook work for him on a regular basis.
Thus, in practice, you would need to hire a Jewish cook. It should be someone who is additionally observant and knowledgeable in the laws of kashrut. If this is not possible and your mother is active, she could help in the process of the food preparation – by doing such acts as turning on the flame or stirring the pot. Even if a Jew does a very minor act of preparation, the prohibition does not apply.
As I mentioned, there are some exceptions to this rule, such as foods which can be eaten without cooking. Thus, for example, if you do have non-Jewish help, they would be able to prepare coffee for your mother since the main part of the coffee is the water, and that of course can be drunk without cooking.
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch Y.D. 113:4; Pri Chadash Y.D. 114:6; Mishnah Halachot XII 16.)
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: The Secret of Happiness Hidden in the Sukkah
questions.question: The Secret of Happiness Hidden in the Sukkah

answers.text:
The Israelites left Egypt with no food, no water and no plan. Then they stumbled on a campsite that had been waiting for them.
The Torah calls Sukkot "the time of our joy." This is the festival meant to teach us how to be happy in the world.
Strangely, though, we don't do anything obviously happy. We leave our homes and move into a sukkah, a hut with a roof so flimsy it isn't even waterproof. What does that have to do with happiness?
The Book of Leviticus (23:43) explains the reason for the holiday: "So that your future generations will know that I placed the Children of Israel in sukkot (huts) when I took them out of the land of Egypt."
There's just one problem. The Torah never describes the Israelites living in sukkot when God took them out of Egypt. Throughout the 40 years in the desert, whenever the Torah mentions where they lived, it's always an ohel, a tent. Never a sukkah.
So how do we make sense of this? I want to share an idea I find very exciting, but first, one more critical question.
The Talmud says that when God speaks of placing us in sukkot, it could mean either physical huts, which the Torah never mentions, or the Clouds of Glory, which it does. A special cloud surrounded the people and protected them on their journey through the desert. But how does a hut connect to a cloud?
I said the Torah never mentions the Israelites dwelling in sukkot. But if we read carefully, there is one moment where it does. The Torah tells us they traveled to a place called Sukkot: "The Children of Israel journeyed from Ramses to Sukkot" (Exodus 12:37).
Why would a place be called Sukkot? Interestingly, the Torah mentions another place with the same name, in a completely different region. When Jacob returns to the Land of Israel, he too comes to a place called Sukkot.
Bible critics argued that the Egyptian Sukkot must be a mistake. We can locate it on the map. Today it's known as Tjeku, and excavations show there was no settlement there when the Israelites left Egypt. It wasn't a city.
James Hoffmeier, one of the world's leading experts in Egyptian archaeology, says the critics have it backwards. Of course the Israelites wouldn't escape Egyptian slavery and head straight into an Egyptian city. If Tjeku had been built up, they would have avoided it. They went there precisely because it wasn't.
What Tjeku was, at the time of the Exodus, was an old campsite. In earlier times, Semitic peoples sometimes migrated from Canaan down to Egypt. Travelers needed places with food, water, and people to trade with. Tjeku had been a massive Semitic transit camp.
Now picture the scene. The Israelites are leaving Egypt with no provisions and no idea what lies ahead. Pharaoh has told them to go. Moses has told them to follow him. It's a tremendous leap of faith. They head out into the desert and the questions start: What will we eat? What will we drink? Where will we even sleep tonight?
Suddenly they arrive at an old campsite, full of huts that had been standing there for decades, maybe centuries, along with materials to build more. "In sukkot I made the Israelites dwell when I took them out of Egypt," God says, on that very night.
Imagine being one of those Israelites and seeing a place that had been waiting for you. It was God's way of saying, "I've got you covered. You'll be looked after. You're not taking this journey alone. I'm with you every step of the way." And it was there that the Clouds of Glory descended and carried them through the rest of the journey.
So when we sit in the sukkah, we remember that first night out of Egypt, when God had prepared a place for us and showed us He would carry us forward. And we remember the Clouds of Glory, which came down that day at Sukkot and led us the rest of the way.
This reveals something remarkable. Every place in the Torah called Sukkot is a transit camp, a place you stop on the way somewhere else.
And that's the secret of life. The more we try to stand still, the less life works for us. The more we accept that life is a journey, the more incredible it becomes.
Being on a journey means you're growing. It means you're not trying to stay put. It means you're trying to become a better person. We just had Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur. We had deep moments, powerful dreams, real desire to change. But no one changes in a day. So take those dreams and ask yourself, "Who am I going to be a year from now?" Then, just like the Israelites heading into the desert, begin the journey one step at a time.
What was my dream on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur? Who did I think I could become? Write it down. Set goals. Then start walking. One small step in that direction, then another, then another.
That's where life's true joy lies: in growing, in heading somewhere, in living with meaning and purpose, in actually becoming something. When all we try to do is make ourselves comfortable, there's no deep fulfillment in it. But when we're taking steps, growing, moving toward a destination, that's where simcha, true joy, comes from.
And when we know God is walking with us every step of the way, we know we're on the right path, the path to greatness. We don't need to be perfect. We don't need to have arrived. The joy is in the journey itself.
As we sit in our sukkahs this year, may we travel back in time and feel the magic of that first night. Feel the Israelites' fear, and their elation, knowing they were marching one step at a time, not only out of Egypt toward the Land of Israel, and not only away from their troubles, but toward building all of history. May God accompany each of us on our own journeys, and may this be a true time of simcha, of joy.
answers.author: Rabbi Daniel Rowe

questions.title: The Toy Torah a Soldier Found in Gaza
questions.question: The Toy Torah a Soldier Found in Gaza

answers.text:
Terrorists fleeing Khan Yunis left behind guns, ammunition, and a child's stuffed holiday toy. One Israeli soldier carried it from Gaza to Lebanon to keep a promise.
It’s an incongruous site: An Israeli soldier stands amid the rubble of a building in Lebanon, holding a child's plush Torah scroll.
It is the kind of toy children receive for Simchat Torah, so they can join the joyous dancing with a Torah of their own. This toy Torah scroll traveled through the darkest chapter in recent Jewish history.
After the Hamas invasion and massacre on October 7, 2023, Avi Kramer and his unit were sent into Gaza. He served in the IDF Paratroopers Brigade's 202nd Battalion, known as the Viper Battalion.
Avi's role was search and rescue. If a soldier was wounded, he would enter the firefight and extract him to safety.
For the first months of the war, Avi was stationed inside Gaza, returning to Israel for only a few days each month. Toward the end of 2023, his unit was operating in Khan Yunis, a major Hamas stronghold in the southern Gaza Strip and the hometown of Yahya Sinwar, the architect of the October 7 attack.
Beneath the city, Hamas had built an extensive network of tunnels, weapons facilities and command centers. Israeli hostages were also held there. Avi's unit was in the midst of rooting out terrorists when his fellow soldiers searched a seemingly ordinary apartment.
There were signs that terrorists had been there only a day earlier. Apparently fleeing as the IDF closed in, they left behind guns, ammunition and combat gear.
Then Avi heard a soldier's excited voice crackle over the radio: "I found a child's toy," the soldier called out. "A stuffed Torah scroll.”
Simchat Torah is one of the most joyous days of the Jewish year. Adults dance in synagogue with Torah scrolls, while children wave flags, ride on their parents' shoulders and carry toy Torahs of their own.
On Simchat Torah 2023, that dancing was shattered by sirens, gunfire, murder, and kidnappings.
That plush toy, embroidered with the words "Rejoice and celebrate on Simchat Torah” (Sisu v'simchu b'Simchat Torah), was a remnant of a celebration interrupted, a people attacked – and a childhood violated.
Avi asked the soldiers who had found it if he could keep it. Strictly speaking, it was not a holy object. Yet it was, for him, a silent witness to October 7 and a symbol of everything the terrorists had tried to steal.
“The soldiers agreed to give me the toy as their way of showing appreciation," Avi says.
That day in Khan Yunis, that little Torah was returned to Jewish hands.
No one knows how this child's toy reached Khan Yunis. Had it belonged to a child kidnapped into Gaza? Had a terrorist looted it from Sderot, Be'eri, Kfar Aza, Nir Oz, or another community overrun that morning?
Avi on the vehicle used to evacuate wounded IDF soldiers during combat.
Avi can only speculate about why a terrorist might have taken it. "Perhaps it was a memento," he says, "their way of saying, 'We've defeated the Jewish people who live by the Torah.'"
Yet Avi knew that October 7 was not the end of the story. The Jewish people would reach another Simchat Torah. They would hold the Torah again and, despite the grief, they would dance.
Avi placed the toy in his pack and, a few months later, carried it out of Gaza. Then he made himself a promise: At the next Simchat Torah, I will dance with this Torah.
A few days before Sukkot 2024, Avi was called back to reserve duty, this time to enter Lebanon and fight Hezbollah. He had little time to pack, but he made sure to bring the toy Torah.
At the army base, busy preparing for the mission, Avi had no time to build a proper sukkah, so he assembled a few beams and made a makeshift one.
His unit remained in Lebanon throughout the seven-day Sukkot holiday. Simchat Torah, which followed, was especially painful: it marked the first Hebrew-calendar anniversary of the Hamas massacre. Hostages remained in captivity, families were mourning, communities were displaced, and soldiers continued to fall.
Still, Avi and his fellow soldiers wanted to observe Simchat Torah with dancing. Yet at their makeshift army base, they needed to be very quiet and keep the lights out.
They had no genuine Torah scroll. So they danced in near-silence with the stuffed one. Surrounded by the wreckage of war, Avi fulfilled his promise.
A year later, on Hoshana Rabba 2025, the final 20 living hostages were released from Gaza. The next day, Simchat Torah, Avi celebrated with friends near Meron in northern Israel, a place with special meaning for him: He had been there on the day of the Hamas attack exactly two years earlier.
This time, Avi danced with a real Torah scroll – and with the stuffed one, grieving yet still dancing, carrying the Torah forward. Terrorists could not take ownership of the Jewish story.
That little Torah, carried into Gaza as a trophy of cruelty, was redeemed as a symbol of Jewish determination, resilience, and faith.
"My hope and prayer," Avi says, "is that one day, when I'm married and have a family of my own, my child will dance with that same toy scroll."

questions.title: An Oct 7 Hero's Widow Remarries Her Husband’s Former Commander
questions.question: An Oct 7 Hero's Widow Remarries Her Husband’s Former Commander

answers.text:
Out of the pain of October 7, a young widow found the courage to love again. Her wedding showed what makes the Jewish people unbreakable.
Beneath a wedding canopy near Ma’ale Adumim on June 23, 2026, Miriam stood beside Ofek, preparing to begin a new chapter in her life.
They were surrounded by family, friends, music, and celebration, but also by tears. Present in every heart was the memory of Captain Ori Mordechai Shani, Miriam’s first husband, the father of her little boy, Roi, and a former soldier under Ofek Datan’s command.
Ori was not physically there, yet everyone could feel his presence.
Miriam and Or Shani were a beautiful young couple, deeply in love and filled with dreams for their future. Together, they built a home grounded in faith, devotion, and love. When their son, Roi, was born, they imagined all the ordinary and precious moments their family would share.
Roi was only four months old when their world was shattered.
just 22 years old, Ori served as a platoon commander in the Golani Brigade’s 51st Battalion. On the morning of October 7, Ori and five of his soldiers left the Kissufim IDF outpost for a routine patrol. When Hamas terrorists invaded Israel, they found themselves facing a heavily armed force. Despite limited ammunition and equipment, Ori remained calm and courageous, leading his men through hours of intense fighting and helping prevent the terrorists from advancing toward Kibbutz Kissufim.
Under relentless fire, Ori guided his soldiers safely back to the base to replenish their ammunition. There, however, Ori and one of his soldiers, Sergeant Re’em Batito, were tragically killed in a mortar attack.
In recognition of his extraordinary courage, leadership, and sacrifice, Ori was posthumously promoted to the rank of captain.
In a single moment, Miriam lost the man she loved, the father of her infant son, and the partner with whom she had planned her future. She now had to look into her baby’s eyes, knowing that he would grow up without his father’s embrace, while somehow finding the strength to face each new day.
Some forms of grief are too deep for words. They do not simply disappear with time, they become part of the person who carries them.
Miriam continued to care for Roi and learned to take one-step and then another. She carried Ori with her, not only in photographs and memories, but as a living presence within her heart. She has described the love he left inside her as a love that will never end and will always remain part of who she is.
Miriam found love with Ofek Dotan, who had been Ori’s commander during his training in the Egoz Unit. Ofek understood the depth of her loss and knew that loving Miriam meant making room for Ori’s memory, never competing with it or trying to replace it.
With the loving support of Ori’s family, Miriam chose to open her heart again.
During their wedding ceremony, Ofek addressed Ori. He recalled how Ori had once told him about Miriam, how deeply he loved her and how excited he was to build a home with her.
Ofek thanked Ori for building the “first floor” of that home. He described the life he and Miriam were now creating as a “second floor”, built upon the strong foundations Ori had laid.
It was an extraordinary expression of tenderness and humility - the new home did not erase the first, it rose from it.
That moment captured something profound about the Jewish people.
For centuries, our small nation has endured persecution, exile, terror, and unimaginable loss. Again and again, we have been broken, yet we have refused to remain among the ruins. We have answered death with life, destruction with rebuilding, and hatred with an even greater commitment to love.
Choosing life does not mean forgetting those we have lost. It means carrying them forward with us. Miriam’s love for Ofek does not diminish the love she will always carry for Ori. Her wedding was not the end of her grief; it was her courageous decision not to allow grief to be the end of her story.
It is planting a tree where fire once burned, building a home where another was shattered, and standing beneath a chuppah with tears in our eyes and hope in our hearts.
We do not rise because we were never broken. We rise because, even after being broken, we gather the pieces and begin to build again.
It is an act of faith, an act of defiance, and one of the greatest acts of courage.
Love this: “Ofek understood the depth of her loss and knew that loving Miriam meant making room for Ori’s memory, never competing with it or trying to replace it.“ May they be blessed to continue building with love and happiness.

questions.title: The World Says You're a Jew. Now What?
questions.question: The World Says You're a Jew. Now What?

answers.text:
At NYU, my nephew took a stand and lost friends overnight. He knew why he was targeted but no one ever explained to him why being Jewish was worth it.
On the morning of October 7, 2023, my nephew, a student at NYU, woke up and reached for his phone. His feed was already flooded with posts attacking Israel. He didn't yet know what had happened there.
Only after scrolling through post after post did he piece together what had happened hours earlier. Hamas terrorists had crossed into Israel, murdered some 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and dragged 251 hostages into Gaza.
Like many Jewish college students, he had a Jewish life, but it wasn’t the center of his identity. He attended Jewish events and the occasional Shabbaton, and moved easily between his Jewish and non-Jewish worlds. Being Jewish was part of who he was. He just never assumed it was how other people saw him.
That changed quickly, as other people began drawing the line for him. Within days, posters went up around campus with the faces of the hostages: grandparents, mothers, teenagers, and dozens of children, some of them babies, taken from their homes and held in tunnels under Gaza by Hamas.
The posters appealed to a basic human instinct: whatever anyone thought about the Middle East, surely no one could look at the photograph of a kidnapped four-year-old and feel nothing.
His response triggered a deluge of hate messages, many of them from people he knew and had thought were his friends.
His response triggered a deluge of hate messages, many of them from people he knew and had thought were his friends.
Yet the posters were torn down, again and again. When the university suspended a student for ripping them off the walls, my nephew posted that the school had made the right call.
His response triggered a deluge of hate messages, many of them from people he knew and had thought were his friends. They defended the student who had torn the posters down and called my nephew Islamophobic, as though what bothered him was the student’s religion rather than the sight of kidnapped Jews being stripped off the walls. Many of those friendships ended right there, and the campus environment became so toxic for him that he went abroad the next semester.
When I talked with him afterward, what struck me most was how well he held up. He didn’t fold, and he didn’t quietly wonder whether the crowd had a point. He was shocked that so many educated people had lost the ability to tell right from wrong on something so plain.
He was singled out because he was a Jew. But he had no sense of what being a Jew is for, and why it might be worth everything it was suddenly costing him.
He was singled out because he was a Jew. But he had no sense of what being a Jew is for, and why it might be worth everything it was suddenly costing him.
He knew he had been singled out because he was a Jew. But no one had given him a sense of what being a Jew is for, and why it might be worth everything it was suddenly costing him.
The world has spent the last three years telling Jews, loudly and clearly, that they are Jews. But what is less clear is who gets to decide what it means, the people shouting at them or the Jews themselves? How we answer that question will shape the Jewish future more than any campus policy or election.
For decades after the Holocaust, many Jews, especially in the West, believed that antisemitism had been pushed to the margins. It was ugly and it still existed, but it belonged to cranks and to history. Respectable people didn’t go there.
Then came October 7. Before Israel had buried its dead, and before a single soldier had entered Gaza, crowds were in the streets of major cities, and they had not come to mourn. The old hatred hadn’t disappeared after all; it simply found new expression - in the language of human rights, anti-colonialism and social justice, and with it a new respectability on campuses, in newsrooms and across professional life.
But what it said to Jews was very old. It didn’t matter whether you had ever been to Israel, voted there, or held any opinion about its government. No one asks Chinese-American students to denounce Beijing’s treatment of the Uyghurs before they are welcome at the lunch table, yet Jewish students were expected to disavow the Jewish state as the price of belonging. It has often been said that Israel has become the Jew among the nations; the reverse is just as true, and every Jew is now treated as Israel’s ambassador, whether he signed up for the job or not.
People who had given little thought to what it means to be Jewish were suddenly being asked to account for it by classmates, colleagues and strangers.
People who had given little thought to what it means to be Jewish were suddenly being asked to account for it by classmates, colleagues and strangers.
One of the stranger results of these three years is that people who had given little thought to what it means to be Jewish were suddenly being asked to account for it by classmates, colleagues and strangers, and every one of them has had to decide what to do about it.
In 1946, in the book published in English as Anti-Semite and Jew, Jean-Paul Sartre wrote that “the Jew is one whom other men consider a Jew.” He meant it as part of an attack on antisemitism, and his argument was that the antisemite, in effect, creates the Jew. For a secular Jew, that can feel uncomfortably accurate: you are Jewish because the world won’t let you forget it.
It is also a trap, and Sartre himself came to see it. His account, for all its good intentions, left the Jews nothing of their own, no history, faith or purpose beyond being hated. Late in life, in conversations with his secretary Benny Lévy, who was returning to Judaism, Sartre acknowledged that the Jews have a real history and hope of their own, one no antisemite wrote for them.
If your identity is whatever your enemies say it is, you have handed them the pen.
If your identity is whatever your enemies say it is, you have handed them the pen.
If your identity is whatever your enemies say it is, you have handed them the pen. To a large degree that is what has happened for the past two generations. Much of Diaspora Jewish identity has been built on the Holocaust and on the fight against antisemitism. Remembering is a sacred duty, but when the story you tell your children is mainly about the people who hated you, you have in effect let them write it. A Jewishness built on being hated has little positive to teach your children, and little to offer them except a reason to walk away.
Jewish tradition makes the opposite claim. When the prophet Bilaam was hired to curse Israel, he looked at the people and said instead: Am levadad yishkon, "a nation that dwells alone" (Numbers 23:9). What was meant as a curse came out as a blessing, describing not a people cut off from the world but one whose sense of itself doesn't depend on the world's approval.
An earlier generation went through something similar. The Jews of Persia in the Purim story were comfortable, hobnobbing with the non-Jews in the capital Shushan as they attended the king’s feast. Then Haman described them to the king as “a certain people, scattered and dispersed among the nations, whose laws are different” (Esther 3:8), and a decree for genocide went out to kill “all the Jews, young and old” (3:13). Haman made no distinction between the observant and the assimilated; to him, a Jew was a Jew.
The Talmud (Shabbat 88a) makes a remarkable claim about what happened next. At Sinai, the Jewish people had accepted the Torah under a kind of compulsion, but now in the days of Purim and Achashverosh they accepted it again, freely. This is the meaning of the phrase in the Megillah, kiymu v’kiblu (Esther 9:27), “they upheld and accepted,” which the Talmud reads to mean that they now upheld with love what they had long before accepted more from a sense of fear.
The generation that finally embraced the Torah with a full heart was the very one that had just been told by the most powerful empire on earth that they were Jews and would die for it.
The generation that finally embraced the Torah with a full heart was the very one that had just been told by the most powerful empire on earth that they were Jews and would die for it.
Consider this: the generation that finally embraced the Torah with a full heart was the very one that had just been told by the most powerful empire on earth that they were Jews and would die for it. They could have treated their Jewishness as a liability to be minimized; instead, they answered by defining themselves.
Some Jews have distanced themselves. This is the familiar “As a Jew” declaration, assuring the world that they are not that kind of Jew. Privately, it may be nothing more dramatic than a necklace tucked beneath a shirt or silence in the group chat.
I don't judge anyone who is afraid, but distance buys less than it promises because the people demanding it rarely stop at the first concession.
Others, like my nephew, have stood their ground. That takes real courage, but resistance alone is still reactive. It may carry you through a hostile semester; it is harder to build a Jewish life on, much less pass one to your children.
And some Jews have gone deeper. They stopped asking, “Why do they hate us?” and began asking, ”What is it about being Jewish that has been worth carrying for all these centuries?” They opened a page of Torah or a book of Jewish history, came to a Shabbat table, and went to Israel to stand with family Jews who never thought of themselves as religious are lighting Shabbat candles, baking challah, signing up for classes and turning up at shul for the first time in years. This is the response of Shushan, taking an identity the world forced on us and choosing it for ourselves.
This response lasts because it is built on who you are rather than on who hates you. That identity is yours to create, and every Jew who chooses to learn, to celebrate, to show up, becomes part of a story that has outlasted every enemy who tried to end it.

questions.title: Prayer at Graves of Righteous
questions.question: I often receive emails from different organizations offering that a rabbi will pray for me at this or that great rabbi’s grave. Does it really make a difference where one prays? Isn't praying to a dead rabbi for salvation practically idolatry?

answers.text:
It’s a very important question. The notion of praying at the graves of the righteous is well-established. The Talmud tells us that Caleb, one of the spies sent to inspect the Holy Land, separated from the rest of the group to visit the Cave of the Patriarchs (ma’arat ha’machpailah) in Hebron. He prostrated himself before the cave and said to them “My fathers, plead for mercy for me that I be saved from the evil designs of the spies” (Sotah 34b).
Elsewhere the Talmud mentions a custom to visit a cemetery during times of calamity, such as a drought. The reason, according to one opinion in the Talmud, is so that the dead will ask for mercy for us in Heaven (Ta’anit 16a).
It has likewise been a Jewish custom all throughout the ages to consider the graves of the righteous (kivrei tzaddikim) places of pilgrimage, and to visit there and recite Psalms and prayers. Hassidim even leave notes (kvitlach) by their Rebbe’s grave.
As you point out, though, this must be understood correctly. Praying to a deceased person rather than God is idolatry. He cannot help you, no matter how great he was in his lifetime. What he might be able to do is intercede in heaven on your behalf. Thus, when a person prays at a grave, he should either have in mind that the righteous person (tzaddik) help bring his prayers to God, or even better, he should pray directly to God that He help him in the merit of the tzaddik buried here (Mishna Berurah 559:41, 581:27).
That being said, it may well be more effective to openly and sincerely pray to God for your needs yourself, rather than asking some great rabbi to do it for you. God gives us challenges and hardships in life so that we’ll turn to Him and improve ourselves – rather than that we find a great person to take them away for us.
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Sleeping Facing the Door
questions.question: Is it true that you’re not supposed to sleep with your feet towards the door of your bedroom? Or is this just a superstition?

answers.text:
Such a custom is not brought in Jewish law. However, there are those who are careful not to do this. The basis for it is because in some cemeteries the custom is to bury the dead with their feet facing the entrance of the cemetery. This is done as an affirmation of the belief in the Resurrection of the Dead – that one day, the dead will rise from their graves. They are buried facing the entrance since they will one day rise up and leave.
As a result of this, there are those who have the custom not to sleep in the same manner, as it resembles the way the dead are buried.
(Sources: Pitchei Teshuvah 362:2, Chatam Sofer Y.D. 332.)
answers.author: Rabbi Pinchas Waldman

questions.title: Personal Prayers on Shabbat
questions.question: I’ve heard that we are not allowed to pray on Shabbat except for the standard prayers in the siddur (prayer-book). Is this so, and why? I am recovering from an addiction, and an important part of the program is to pray every day. Would this be okay?

answers.text:
I wish you much success in your recovery first of all. May your prayers be accepted, and may God help you in your efforts.
What you wrote is only partly true. There is a general rule that we may not pray for physical matters on Shabbat, although it is fine to pray for spiritual ones. We are, however, allowed to say the standard Shabbat prayers of the prayer-book (as well as in Birkat HaMazon (Grace After Meals)), even though they include many requests related to physical matters. It is only that we should not add additional personal prayers for non-spiritual needs.
There are two reasons for this brought in Jewish law. One is that it is a form of speaking about our own affairs on Shabbat which the Prophet Isaiah forbade (58:13). The second is that discussing our physical problems is liable to make us sad, which will contradict the spirit of Shabbat.
Neither of these reasons apply to praying for spiritual matters since they are not the mundane matters forbidden by Isaiah, and mentioning them is much less likely to upset us.
One exception to this is praying for a person who is gravely ill. That we may do even on Shabbat since preserving life takes precedence over almost all the laws of the Torah.
In your case it would definitely be proper to pray even on Shabbat. As I’m sure you know, addictions can be quite serious and life-threatening, and it’s important that you keep the healing process going. Since, however, addictions are typically not an immediate danger to life, it is proper to add: “It is Shabbat from crying out, and healing will speedily arrive” (“Shabbat hi mi’lizok, urefuah kerovah la’vo.”) The lead rabbi of this service, Rabbi P Waldman, suggested a beautiful variation of this for you, to add to the end of your prayers:
“Though it is Shabbat, and we may not pray for the ill, I ask for the strength and courage to continue to stay away from addiction, which is the cause of spiritual and physical dangers, and to thereby be relieved of the addiction soon.”
Again, our wishes that you have a complete recovery very soon.
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Haftorah – Source for the Custom
questions.question: What is the source of the custom to read from the Prophets on Shabbat and other occasions after reading from the Torah? Is it a recent custom?

answers.text:
Thank you for raising the interesting topic. On many days on which the Torah is read – Shabbat and the major festivals, as well as on fast days in the afternoon (at the Mincha prayer), a short selection from the Prophets is read, on a topic relating to the Torah reading and/or the occasion. It is known as the haftorah (sometimes written haftarah in English). A blessing is recited beforehand and blessings are recited after. Preferably the haftorah should be read from a scroll, written in a manner similar to a Torah.
As an aside, it isn’t that clear what the word “haftorah” actually means. (Note that although the word looks like “Torah”, the ‘t’ sound in it comes from the letter ‘tet’ – unlike “Torah” which is spelled with a ‘tav’.) The root of the word is “patar” – which might mean to exempt or dismiss (common in Rabbinical Hebrew; see also I Samuel 19:10, II Chronicles 23:8), or to open/begin (Exodus 13:2, Psalms 22:8, Proverbs 17:14).
Some suggest that haftorah relates to “exempt” because it was instituted at a time when the Greek authorities forbade Torah study (see below). Since the Jews were “exempt” from reading the Torah in the synagogue due to the danger, they read from the Prophets instead (Avudraham, Seder Shacharis Shel Shabbat; Levush 284:1).
An alternate suggestion is that it relates to “dismiss” because the congregation was then “dismissed” from the earlier part of the service – the Torah reading – now continuing with the Prophets and then the Mussaf prayer (Avudraham, Hirsch Siddur).
A third suggestion is that it relates to “open” – likewise because it marked the start of a new part of the services – possibly to distinguish between the more significant Torah and the words of the Prophets (Aruch HaShulchan 284:1).
It is not known exactly when the practice of reading the haftorah was instituted, but it is definitely an ancient custom, from well before the period of the Mishna (put in final form in the early third century CE, based on the teachings of several generations of rabbis, spanning from the late Second Temple era). The Mishna makes ample reference to such a custom (see esp. Megillah Ch. 3) – which was clearly already in practice in virtually all its detail. In addition, the fact that we recite blessings both before and after reading the haftorah indicates that it is a universal and Rabbinically-sanctioned practice, rather than an optional custom.
(There are actually two probable references to the synagogue reading of the Prophets found in the New Testament (Acts 13:15 and Luke 4:17), implying the practice dates from at least the Second Temple period.)
What selection from the Prophets is read for each haftorah? The Talmud (Megillah 31) lists all of the special haftorah readings, such as for the holidays. For ordinary Shabbats, though, there is no ancient established tradition. The general rule is that the haftorah should been on a topic in some way related to the Torah reading (Shulchan Aruch 284:1). Beyond that, different segments of Israel have different customs (Ashkenazi, Sephardic, Yemenite, Italian, Polish, German, etc.). There is much overlap between the various customs, but there are many discrepancies as well.
What is the basis for reading the haftorah? No reason is given in any Talmudic-era source. The most well-known suggested reason is that during the era of Greek oppression (leading up to the Chanukah story), the public reading of the Torah was forbidden. In place of it, Jews began reading from the Prophets instead. Later, the decree was relaxed, but the Jews maintained their new custom to read from the Prophets as well. (Many authorities quote this reason. The earliest mention of it I found was in Sefer Avudraham, a commentary on the prayers written by R. Dovid Avudraham in the early 14th century.)
Another early source states that reading from the Prophets was a part of the decree of Ezra the Scribe to read from the Torah on various occasions (Sefer HaMachria 31, by R’ Yeshaya di Trani, of 13th century Italy). A more recent suggestion is that it was instituted in response to heretical sects such as the Samaritans, which denied the sanctity of the prophetic books (R. Hirsh, R. Reuven Margolios).
Before reading the haftorah an extra section from the Torah is read, called maftir. On Shabbat and holidays, this is not one of main aliyot – the 5-7 people called for reading the Torah. It is an additional section read immediately before the Prophets, instituted by the Sages to indicate that the words of the Prophets are not as central as the Torah itself (Talmud Megillah 23a). On a typical Shabbat, the last few verses of the weekly portion are reread. On special Shabbats and on holidays, a special reading is read, relevant to the occasion.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Damages Done by Children
questions.question: Our neighbor’s 8-year-old son borrowed a toy and broke it. Should we make an issue of it? Are our neighbors obligated to pay us back?

answers.text:
Well, you should definitely tell the parents, since they should teach their children to be more careful with other people’s property.
In terms of paying back, technically, neither a child nor his parents have to pay for his damages. The Mishna (Baba Kama 8:4) states regarding children (below Bar/Bat Mitzvah) that “their contact is bad” – because if you damage them you’re obligated in compensation, while if they damage you they are exempt (since as minors, they are not responsible for their actions). Parents also have no technical obligation vis-à-vis their children’s damages – though it is nice if they do offer to pay.
If a child steals an item and the item still exists (unlike, say, if he steals candy and eats it or if he borrows something and breaks or loses it), the item must be returned since it still belongs to its original owner (Shulchan Aruch C.M. 349:3).
When a child grows up, it is considered meritorious for him to compensate all damages he did when he was a child, as part of his repentance (see Rashi to Bava Kama 98b s.v. “v’achpiyai”, Shulchan Aruch O.C. 343:1, Mishna Berurah 343:9).

questions.title: Separation between Fish and Meat
questions.question: I was recently invited for Shabbat dinner. It was a wonderful, uplifting experience. One thing I was unfamiliar with is that everyone was told to take a drink between the fish and the chicken. I am familiar with separating between meat and milk, but not meat and fish. Can you give me some guidelines about this?

answers.text:
The separation we make between meat and fish is actually based on a health concern. The Talmud (Pesachim 76b) writes that eating meat and fish cooked together is harmful to one’s health (and also causes bad breath). (I've heard that some actually find that the combination these two types of proteins is difficult to digest.) Although some later authorities have noted that we are not familiar with any such health issues today, practically speaking, we make a small separation between the fish and meat courses of a meal. To ensure that the meat and fish do not come in contact with one another:
(a) We serve the fish on a separate plate and eat it with a separate fork.
(b) We take a drink between the fish and meat course. (It needs not be alcoholic, although some take the opportunity to make a “l’chaim” at this point during the meal.)
(c) We eat a little bit – such as a few bites of challah – between the fish and meat course. (see Rema Yoreh Deah 116:3)
One of the important messages of this is that Judaism is equally concerned for our physical as our spiritual well-being. Deuteronomy 4:15 states, “You shall be very careful with yourselves” – which many take figuratively to mean we must care for our health (see Talmud - Brachot 32b). We take seriously as remote a health concern as consuming meat and fish together; all the more so visible dangers.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Completion of Kaddish
questions.question: My father passed away on June 14, which was 24 Sivan, but was not buried until the Sunday after, 27 Sivan. Until when should I recite the kaddish?

answers.text:
Following the passing of a parent, Kaddish is recited for 11 months as a merit for his/her soul. Although the Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 17a) writes that for the most wicked, judgment in purgatory may extend as long as 12 months, we recite Kaddish for only 11 months so as not to imply our parent was evil (Rema 376:4).
The 11 months are counted from the date of the deceased’s burial rather than his passing (Bi’ur Halacha 132). In your case, Kaddish would end at the end of the day of 26 Iyar (May 6), after the Mincha prayers.
Note that Sephardic Jews have a different custom. They recite Kaddish for 11 months, then stop for a week, and then continue to complete the year. Also, if the deceased was a sinner, we do say Kaddish for a full 12 months.
In general, if you need to check Hebrew dates, you can refer to the aish.com calendar.
Here is an interesting account of saying the Kaddish: http://www.aish.com/sp/so/My-11-Months-of-Kaddish.html.
May your father’s soul be blessed.
(Sources: Shulchan Aruch Y.D. 376:4; Igrot Moshe Y.D. IV 16; Yalkut Yosef, Aveilut 40, fn. 22.)
answers.author: Aish.com Staff

questions.title: Earliest Time for Morning Prayers (Shacharit)
questions.question: I’ve noticed that our synagogue has morning services (Shacharit) quite early during the workweek, after which most of the congregants hurry off to work. During the winter months it is still dark outside for most of the services. Shouldn’t morning services be held when it is daytime already?

answers.text:
What you describe is a fairly universal practice – very early morning services after which the congregants hurry off – trying their best to beat rush hour traffic. However, yes, there are a few issues in Jewish law of concern.
There are 3 relevant times when discussing the earliest times for morning prayers. I list them here together with the prayers which may be said at each time:
(a) Dawn – when the first light of day appears on the horizon. The blessings and prayers at the beginning of morning services may be said at this time. (In truth most of the morning blessings and according to many, pesukei d'zimra may be said even before dawn.) This is roughly 90 minutes before sunrise (more on the precise times below).
(b) Partial light - when one can recognize an acquaintance standing 4 cubits (6-8 feet) away (Talmud Brachot 9b). This is the earliest time for reciting the Shema, the first blessing preceding the Shema, and for donning Tallit and Tefillin (Shulchan Aruch 18:3, 30:1 & 58:1; see also Biur Halacha s.v. “b’lo brachot”). This is roughly 50 minutes before sunrise.
(c) Sunrise: This is the ideal time to recite the Shemoneh Esrei (Amidah), beginning it the moment of sunrise. It should preferably not be recited before this time. It is also permissible to recite Shemoneh Esrei for the first 4 hours of the day (Shulchan Aruch 89:1).
Regarding the Shemoneh Esrei, there is one important exception. One who is about to embark on a journey (and in Talmudic times would have no choice but to take the outgoing caravan), may recite Shemoneh Esrei from dawn (Shulchan Aruch 89:8). Contemporary rabbis extend this to people who have need to commute to work early, even though they do so on a daily basis (see e.g. Igrot Moshe O.C. 4:6).
Putting all of this together, a synagogue may have early Shacharit services (beginning after dawn), but they must be mindful of a few things:
(a) People should not put on their Tallit or Tefillin or begin the blessings of the Shema until the time of “partial light.” Many congregations which want to start as early as possible will begin services before that time, and then right after Yishtabach (before the blessings of Shema) put on Tallit and Tefillin and continue. In other congregations, the congregants put on Tallit and Tefillin without a blessing at the start, and then after Yishtabach touch each of them and recite the appropriate blessings (Rema 18:3; Shulchan Aruch 30:3). (First touch the Tallit strings and recite a blessing on it, then touch the Tefillin boxes and recite the blessings on them.) I feel the first method is preferable since when following the second, people not familiar with the issues will put on their Tallit and Tefillin with the blessings too early.
(b) All of the above is not advisable for someone who does not have early work obligations. Someone who does not need to commute to work early but who just wants to get an early start on his day should really not attend services which recite Shemoneh Esrei before sunrise.
When exactly are all of these times? The best and most accurate resource for worldwide times is myzmanim.com.
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: Tefillin on Top of Bandage
questions.question: I need to have a minor operation on my left arm next week. It will be bandaged for at least a week afterwards. This is the arm I place my Tefillin on. Am I allowed to place my Tefillin on top of the bandage?

answers.text:
In general, Tefillin must be placed directly against one’s skin (or for the head Tefillin, one’s hair), without anything in between. In a case such as yours where this is impossible, we rely on a minority opinion that Tefillin does not need to be directly against the skin. Thus, you would place your Tefillin on top of the bandage, trying your best to estimate its correct location (Shulchan Aruch 27:5, Mishnah Berurah 17).
Since this is against the majority opinion, there are a few differences in how you should put on your Tefillin:
(a) You should cover up your arm-Tefillin, say with the sleeve of a sweater or jacket. This is a precaution instituted by the Sages so that others won’t see what you’re doing and do so themselves – even when their arm or head is not bandaged (Shulchan Aruch 27:5).
(b) In terms of reciting the blessings on your Tefillin, since most opinions hold that Tefillin must be directly against the skin, you should act as if you are only wearing head-Tefillin. This means that if you are a Sefardi – who generally recites only one blessing on both the arm- and head-Tefillin – “l’hani’ach Tefillin” (and only the second blessing (“al mitzvat Tefillin”) if something goes wrong with the first), you should recite the second blessing only.
If you are Ashkenazi, who normally recites both blessings on both parts of the Tefillin, you should recite both blessings, but only when putting on your head-Tefillin (Shulchan Aruch and Rema, 26:2).
One other point: If the bandage does not cover where the Tefillin box or the knot in the back goes, even if it covers the straps you use to fasten the box, you can wear your Tefillin and recite the blessings as normal (Rema 27:4, Mishnah Berurah 16).
Finally, my wishes that your operation goes smoothly and you merit a speedy recovery!
answers.author: Rabbi Dovid Rosenfeld

questions.title: “Who Did Not Make Me a Woman”
questions.question: I was born the oldest daughter of a mostly secular Jewish family and became observant in my early adulthood. I love everything about Judaism and my new life. However, to this day I am bothered by the blessing men recite daily in their morning prayers – “Blessed are You… who did not make me a woman.” It just seems so demeaning! How does that jibe with everything else Judaism teaches about the importance and special role of women?

answers.text:
I sympathize with your frustration. After teaching us so many positive messages about the central role women play in Judaism, the Sages go ahead and institute a blessing where men thank God they were not creating as women! How does that fit with everything else we are taught? Are the Sages really chauvinists in disguise?
However, most people badly misunderstand the meaning of this blessing. In fact, there is nothing demeaning about it. It actually reveals the profound wisdom of our Sages.
The idea is as follows.
Kabbalistically, a woman’s body is considered spiritually higher than a man’s. At the creation, Adam was created directly from the earth. Eve, by contrast, was created from a part of Adam – one step further removed from the physical world.
As a result, a woman’s physical side is loftier than that of a man, a closer reflection of the spiritual world from which it derives. This can be borne out in many ways. Here are a few examples:
(a) Women tend to be more repulsed by disgusting objects or vulgar behavior than men – such as insects, blood, and obscene behavior. Being more spiritual, they find the coarsest aspects of the physical world more repellant.
(b) Women are typically more attractive than men – meaning, their physical side is a closer reflection of their spiritual. The Torah likewise tells us that our matriarchs were especially beautiful. Their inner spiritual beauty was more strongly reflected on the physical plane than that of their male counterparts.
A different way of stating this is that women have greater body-soul harmony than men. Their bodies are naturally closer and more attuned to their souls. Conversely, men, in spite of the loftiness of their souls, have bodies much more liable to stoop to vulgar, depraved behavior. A casual reading of the news on any day will readily confirm that men are far more likely than women to be involved in vicious, sordid crime.
However, as with all issues, there are two ways of looking at this. Since men have a much greater discrepancy between soul and body, it is much harder for them to control their bodies. But as a result, when they do, they have accomplished much more than women – and have perfected their souls much more in the process.
Getting back to our question, the blessing “who has not made me a woman” is part of a series. Men recite three blessings, in the following order – “who has not made me a non-Jew,” “who has not made me a slave,” and “who has not made me a woman.” This succession reflects who has more mitzvot (commandments).
